questions.stem: What is described as the new name of a Pilot?
questions.explanation: The new name of Pilot is MVP; it is the next stage after Prototyping.

questions.stem: What is considered and used in an MVP?
options: A subset of requirements, real data, hardware, software and a limited number of features
The complete set of requirements with full production hardware
Only dummy data with no real requirements
Every feature, but with no infrastructure
Full software licences with no data
questions.explanation: In an MVP a subset of actual requirements, a subset of real data, a subset of hardware and infrastructure, a subset of software and a limited number of features are used.

questions.stem: Who uses an MVP once it is ready?
options: Actual users, giving business users a taste of the real solution
questions.explanation: Once an MVP is ready it is released to actual users to start using, giving business users a taste of the actual solution.

questions.stem: What is the biggest advantage of the MVP approach?
options: It removes the need for testing
With a small implementation and small investment, the business can decide whether to go to the next stage or drop the solution
It guarantees the solution will succeed in Production
It eliminates the need for data governance
It requires no infrastructure at all
questions.explanation: With a small implementation and small investment, the business can taste the solution and decide to go to the next stage or drop it.

questions.stem: How do many organisations now divide a complete solution using MVPs?
options: By building the whole solution in one release
By outsourcing every MVP to a different vendor
By implementing the solution in chunks as multiple MVPs, supported by the Agile approach
By building one MVP per employee
questions.explanation: Many organisations divide a complete solution into multiple MVPs, implementing in chunks, which is supported by the Agile approach where the product matures over shorter timeframes.

questions.stem: Which three environments are spun up in an MVP, just like an actual implementation?
questions.explanation: In an MVP, three environments are spun up, DEV, UAT and PROD, along with all the steps required to go to Production.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed among the steps included in an MVP?
questions.explanation: The MVP includes DevOps, CI/CD, Metadata Management, Data Quality, Data Governance, Data Lineage and Master and Reference Data Management; sales commission calculation is not listed.

questions.stem: Why does going with an MVP approach make sense in the current era?
options: Because business models change frequently, technologies change quarterly and recessions hit every now and then
Because business users no longer need to test
questions.explanation: In an era where business models change frequently, technologies change quarterly and recessions hit every now and then, the MVP approach makes sense.

questions.stem: Which testing and environments are built in the MVP stage, and at what scale?
options: UT is done and SIT, UAT and Production environments are built, but on a small scale for business users
No testing until the productionised solution
questions.explanation: In the MVP stage UT is done and SIT, UAT and Production environments are built, but on a small scale for business users.

questions.stem: How does an MVP differ from a Prototype in terms of who tests the end solution?
options: In both stages only technical folks test the solution
In an MVP only the sales team tests the solution
In a Prototype business users test, in an MVP developers test
In both stages only business users test the solution
In a Prototype technical folks test the tools and solution, whereas an MVP is released to actual users
questions.explanation: MVP is the stage after Prototyping, where tools and technologies were tested by technical folks; the MVP is then released to actual users.
